analysis: Minimum risk: Solver concentrates in the lowest-volatility, weakly correlated assets — about 69% US Treasuries (SABE), 23% North American large caps (WPETF) and 8% IG corporates (KUSIG). Volatility falls to about 4.1%, below any single ETF (lowest is KUSIG at 5.1%), because SABE is negatively correlated with equities. Expected return is about 5.3%.

Maximum return: with only the sum-to-1 and no-short-selling constraints, Solver puts 100% in the single highest-returning ETF, WPETF (about 15.0% return at 12.3% volatility). This shows that a pure return objective abandons diversification entirely.

12% target volatility: this sits just below WPETF's own risk, so Solver keeps about 98% in WPETF and adds about 2% KUSIG to trim volatility to exactly 12%, earning about 14.8%. This portfolio lies on the efficient frontier.

15% and 18% targets: in a long-only portfolio the highest-return mix (100% WPETF) has only 12.3% volatility, so any higher risk target can only be reached by adding riskier but lower-returning assets. Solver blends WPETF with Emerging Markets (LPEM): about 41/59 for 15% (return about 10.2%) and 3/97 for 18% (return about 7.1%). These portfolios take more risk for less return — they are below the efficient frontier, and a rational investor would not choose them.

Key takeaway: the long-only efficient frontier runs only from about 4.1% volatility (minimum risk) to about 12.3% (maximum return). Targets inside that range give efficient portfolios, while targets above it are inefficient. Reaching 15–18% volatility efficiently would require short selling or leverage, which the fully invested, no-leverage constraint rules out. (If short selling were permitted, Solver reaches roughly 25% return at 15% volatility and 29% at 18%, but only with large short positions of 200–300% in Treasuries.)

Method note: targeting a volatility with an equality constraint is non-convex, so GRG Nonlinear can stop at a local optimum depending on the starting weights. The weights shown were confirmed with a multistart search; using Solver's Multistart option reproduces them.
